items.title: Quality assurance and quality control are different things
items.claim: A car plant inspects every vehicle at the end of the line and rejects defective units. Which approach is this?

options.text: Quality assurance, because it ensures quality
Quality control — defect detection after the fact. Quality assurance builds quality into the process so defects don't arise

items.reveal:
W. Edwards Deming, who worked in postwar Japan, argued that inspecting defects out is more expensive than preventing them. His '14 Points' for management (1986) included 'cease dependence on inspection to achieve quality'.

Toyota's andon-cord system stops the line whenever a worker sees a problem — quality is built upstream. Quality control still happens, but as a back-stop, not the main mechanism. ISO 9001 audits processes (assurance), not products (control).
items.why: Two firms with identical defect rates can have very different cost structures depending on whether defects are prevented or caught.

items.title: High gearing is risk, not failure
items.claim: A firm has long-term debt of £40 million and equity of £60 million. Its gearing ratio (debt / debt+equity) is 40%. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Gearing this high is always dangerous
Higher gearing magnifies returns to shareholders in good times and losses in bad — utilities routinely run 60%+ because cash flows are stable
Equity is always cheaper than debt

items.reveal:
UK water and electricity utilities (Severn Trent, National Grid) often carry gearing above 60% because regulated cash flows make debt servicing predictable. Tech firms (pre-2022) often had near-zero gearing because cash flows were volatile and equity was cheap.

Modigliani and Miller (1958) argued that, in perfect markets, capital structure is irrelevant. In real markets — with taxes, bankruptcy costs and asymmetric information — there is an optimal range. Lehman Brothers' gearing reached above 30:1 (debt:equity) before its 2008 collapse.
items.why: Whether high gearing is reckless depends on what cash flows look like. The number alone tells you little.

items.title: Herzberg's hygiene factors don't motivate
items.claim: Frederick Herzberg's 1959 'Motivation to Work' surveyed 200 engineers and accountants. What did he conclude about pay?

options.text: Pay is a 'hygiene factor' — low pay causes dissatisfaction but high pay does not produce sustained motivation. Motivators are achievement, recognition and the work itself
Pay had no effect either way
Only senior staff are motivated by pay

items.reveal:
Herzberg's two-factor theory splits job factors into hygiene (pay, conditions, supervision, policies) — whose absence causes dissatisfaction — and motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) — which actively drive engagement.

Methodological critics note Herzberg used the 'critical incident' interview technique, in which people tend to attribute good experiences to themselves and bad ones to external factors. Replications using other methods get less crisp results.
items.why: Pay rises buy off dissatisfaction, not loyalty or effort. Most modern HR practice combines compensation (hygiene) with job design (motivators) — a direct legacy of Herzberg.
